paragraphs: Equivariant networks build assumptions about symmetry directly into their architecture: transforming an input produces a corresponding transformation in its features. This paper asks how that architectural choice relates to generalization, meaning performance beyond the training data. It studies networks whose feature transformations are specified through mathematical group representations.

The authors analyze how perturbations affect each layer in the Fourier domain and use this analysis to derive norm-based PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds. These bounds connect generalization error to several design choices: the size of the symmetry group, the dimensions of its irreducible representations, and how many times those representations appear in the network.

The resulting theory offers guidance for choosing how a network represents symmetry, rather than treating equivariance as a single architectural switch. In general, the bound favors larger groups, and numerical experiments support that tendency. The finding is a relationship expressed through the bound and supported empirically, rather than an unconditional promise that increasing symmetry always improves every model.
neurips-2022-a-pac-bayesian-generalizati.tldr: A PAC-Bayesian analysis connects equivariant networks’ generalization to symmetry-group size and representation choices.

paragraphs: Several brain regions can influence behavior simultaneously, each following a different control policy. This creates a learning problem for the basal ganglia: the actions an animal takes may come partly or entirely from another controller. The paper proposes a biologically plausible reinforcement-learning model that can learn under this arrangement.

Its key prediction is that dopamine combines reward prediction error with action surprise, which measures how unexpected an action is under the basal ganglia’s current policy. Adding this term makes the model implement an approximate form of Q-learning. In navigation and reaching experiments, it learns from behavior generated partly or completely by other policies; models without the term struggle or fail in those settings.

The model also provides a computational explanation for several observed dopamine patterns, including movement-related activity decreasing with practice and differences between dorsal and ventral striatum. These are explanatory successes of a proposed model. It additionally makes predictions for future dopamine recordings, connecting the learning mechanism to further biological tests.
neurips-2022-action-modulated-midbrain-d.tldr: A dopamine model combining reward prediction error with action surprise explains how the basal ganglia could learn from other controllers’ actions.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty using a posterior distribution over model parameters. This paper studies what happens to that posterior as more data become available. Its theoretical setting assumes that the true regression function belongs to a Besov space, a function class used here to describe the target’s regularity.

For a network with a spike-and-slab prior, the authors prove posterior consistency and a near-minimax optimal convergence rate. Consistency means that the posterior increasingly concentrates around the true regression function. The rate describes how quickly this happens and is close to the best worst-case rate for the relevant function class.

The result also adapts to unknown smoothness: the convergence rate does not worsen merely because the function’s smoothness is not supplied in advance. The authors then establish the same rate for a shrinkage prior, which they describe as more computationally feasible. This connects a more practical prior choice to the same asymptotic statistical guarantee within the studied setting.
neurips-2022-asymptotic-properties-for-b.tldr: Bayesian neural networks with spike-and-slab or shrinkage priors achieve near-optimal posterior convergence for regression functions in Besov spaces.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation concerns adapting a model to a new domain without using the original source data. This paper approaches the task as unsupervised clustering. Its guiding intuition is that examples close together in the model’s feature space should receive more similar predictions than examples that are farther apart.

The proposed prediction-consistency objective encourages agreement among local neighbors while encouraging different predictions for more distant features. These two pressures support both the formation of feature clusters and their assignment to predictions. To make training efficient, the authors optimize an upper bound on the objective that reduces to two simple terms.

The paper also connects existing approaches in domain adaptation and contrastive learning through their treatment of discriminability and diversity. Experiments report superior performance for the proposed method, supporting its use as a simple baseline. Adaptations to source-free open-set and partial-set settings further demonstrate its applicability beyond the main setting, without establishing that one configuration works universally across all domain shifts.
neurips-2022-attracting-and-dispersing-a.tldr: Encouraging nearby features to agree and distant features to disagree yields a simple, effective source-free adaptation method.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are widely used to assign labels to nodes, but evaluation on a limited collection of benchmark graphs gives an incomplete picture of their behavior. This paper investigates performance through synthetic graphs whose characteristics can be controlled, allowing a finer-grained examination of where different GNNs succeed or struggle.

The study varies four properties: whether node classes are balanced, whether edges tend to connect nodes of the same or different classes, whether node attributes are biased or random, and whether graphs are small or large. Controlling these properties provides a way to examine particular aspects of a graph instead of relying only on comparisons between existing datasets.

The authors report that these experiments clarify GNN strengths and weaknesses across the studied characteristics. The contribution is an evaluation framework and empirical analysis, rather than a new node-classification architecture. A publicly released codebase lets researchers evaluate different GNNs on generated graphs, extending the same style of controlled investigation to future methods.
neurips-2022-beyond-real-world-benchmark.tldr: Controlled synthetic graphs reveal how node-classification GNNs behave as class balance, connectivity, attributes, and graph size change.

paragraphs: Inverse halftoning reconstructs continuous-tone images from printed dot patterns. Existing supervised reconstruction methods can produce visible artifacts when test images use dithering patterns that differ substantially from training examples. This matters because both the halftoning algorithm and its settings can change the patterns a reconstruction model encounters.

The paper addresses this problem by generating more varied halftones for training. Its Conditional Diffusion model for image Halftoning treats black pixels as moving particles and guides them through a reverse diffusion process. Changing the initial state produces different patterns while conditioning on image gray levels and a Laplacian prior.

A meta-halftone guided network adds blue-noise guidance to discourage redundant patterns and unwanted artifacts. The resulting diversity exposes the inverse model to a broader range of halftone distributions, helping it learn a more robust mapping back to continuous tones. Quantitative and visual evaluations report state-of-the-art results, supporting the strategy of improving reconstruction through better-controlled variation in its training inputs.
neurips-2022-conditional-diffusion-proce.tldr: A conditional diffusion model generates diverse halftone patterns to improve image reconstruction on unfamiliar dithering styles.

paragraphs: Recovering an equation from data requires finding both its symbolic structure and its numerical coefficients. Neural approaches can tackle this task, but their nonconvex optimization complicates guarantees about recovering the exact equation. CoNSoLe separates recovery into two stages and seeks convexity in each under the paper’s stated mild conditions.

The first stage searches for the right symbols using a modified deep Q-learning procedure. It maintains convexity of both the negative Q-function and the negative reward function at each iteration. This yields a provably convex negative optimal Q-function for learning the true connections between symbols.

Given an exact symbolic search result, the second stage uses a Locally Convex equation Learning network to estimate coefficients. For commonly used physical functions, the authors characterize a large region where its loss is strictly convex. This is a conditional, local guarantee rather than unrestricted global convexity of the entire recovery problem. Experiments on diverse datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches.
neurips-2022-console-convex-neural-symbo.tldr: CoNSoLe separates equation discovery into symbol search and coefficient fitting, establishing convexity properties under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Value iteration computes values for states by repeatedly considering their possible actions. Updating one state at a time already avoids the need to finish a full batch of state updates. However, ordinary asynchronous value iteration still searches the complete action set for each update, which becomes expensive when many actions are available.

Doubly-Asynchronous Value Iteration extends the same computational flexibility to actions. Each update maximizes over a sampled subset of actions, with a subset size chosen by the user. This reduces the work required for an individual update without waiting for a complete sweep through the action space.

The authors prove convergence to the optimal value function with probability one and a near-geometric convergence rate with probability at least one minus delta. They also establish a computation-time guarantee for obtaining a near-optimal policy that nearly matches a previous value-iteration bound. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness, showing that sampled action updates can retain strong theoretical properties while making updates less costly.
neurips-2022-doubly-asynchronous-value-i.tldr: DAVI samples actions during value updates while retaining probability-one convergence and strong convergence-rate guarantees.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, but sampling often requires hundreds or thousands of sequential neural-network evaluations. DPM-Solver addresses this cost by treating generation as solving a diffusion ordinary differential equation and designing a numerical method specifically for that equation’s structure.

The authors derive an exact solution formulation that handles the linear component analytically. A change of variables then expresses the remaining computation as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network. This formulation supports a high-order numerical solver with a convergence-order guarantee. The exact formulation underlies the solver; it does not mean that a finite-step numerical sample is exact.

The method works with both discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models without further training. Experiments report high-quality samples using 10 to 20 network evaluations and speedups of four to sixteen times over previous state-of-the-art training-free samplers. The contribution is a sampling improvement for existing models, demonstrating how exploiting the equation’s structure can substantially reduce generation cost.
neurips-2022-dpm-solver-a-fast-ode-solve.tldr: DPM-Solver exploits diffusion equations’ structure to generate high-quality samples in 10–20 network evaluations without additional training.

paragraphs: Participants in federated learning can have data of very different quality and distribution. A shared model may therefore hurt some participants even while satisfying familiar fairness measures. This paper frames shared-model learning as a public decision problem and uses cooperative game theory to define fairness through core stability.

Under this definition, no subset of participants should gain sufficiently by forming its own coalition, with the comparison accounting for the coalition’s share of all participants. Core-stable predictors are robust to low-quality local data and satisfy proportionality and Pareto optimality. These properties give each participant a minimum share of achievable utility and rule out improvements for one participant that cost nobody else.

The proposed CoreFed protocol finds core-stable predictors for convex losses and approximate core-stable predictors for nonconvex losses such as those of smooth neural networks. The paper also establishes existence in more general settings. On two real-world datasets, CoreFed achieves better core-stability fairness than FedAvg while maintaining similar accuracy, supporting this coalition-based fairness criterion empirically.
neurips-2022-fairness-in-federated-learn.tldr: CoreFed promotes federated-learning fairness by seeking shared models that participants cannot substantially improve upon by forming smaller coalitions.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning systems can send intermediate features from resource-limited devices to the cloud for continued training. When bandwidth is scarce, this traffic becomes a bottleneck. The paper argues that compressing individual feature values misses structure that could make those transmissions substantially smaller.

Stripe-wise Group Quantization uses similarities both across feature channels and across spatial positions. It reorganizes features according to inter-channel similarity and encodes their structure at both levels. The method also bounds the gradient deviation introduced by quantization, connecting its compression mechanism to the behavior of learning rather than considering transmission size alone.

The authors establish a sublinear convergence order like that of ordinary stochastic-gradient optimization. Experiments report an improvement of up to 15.97 times in traffic reduction ratio and a 9.22-times image-processing speedup over uniform quantized training. They also report adequate accuracy comparable to FP32 training even with four-bit quantization. These results support structured feature compression as a way to reduce communication costs while preserving useful training performance.
neurips-2022-hierarchical-channel-spatia.tldr: Stripe-wise Group Quantization compresses channel and spatial feature structure to reduce collaborative-learning traffic while preserving useful accuracy.

paragraphs: Causal discovery becomes harder when some causes are unobserved. This paper studies a particularly structured version of that problem: hidden variables form a hierarchy, their children may also be hidden, and only the leaf variables are measured. The graph can contain multiple paths between variables, so it need not be a tree.

The proposed estimation procedure uses rank-deficiency constraints among the measured variables to infer the hidden structure. These constraints provide information for locating latent variables, determining their cardinalities, and identifying how they are arranged. The approach therefore seeks information about an entire hidden hierarchy from relationships visible at its observed leaves.

The recovery guarantee requires linear causal relationships and appropriate restrictions on graph structure. Under those conditions, the algorithm asymptotically identifies the correct Markov equivalence class of the whole graph. That qualification matters: the theorem recovers the graph up to the stated equivalence, rather than necessarily identifying one uniquely oriented graph from finite data. Its scope nevertheless extends beyond tree-shaped latent structures.
neurips-2022-latent-hierarchical-causal-.tldr: Rank constraints can recover latent causal hierarchies up to Markov equivalence asymptotically under linearity and graph restrictions.

paragraphs: Conventional convolution kernels arrange their weights on a regular grid. Enlarging such a kernel increases its parameter count quadratically, encouraging networks to use small kernels with limited local coverage. This paper proposes a different way to organize the region examined by a single convolutional layer.

A log-polar space convolution uses an elliptical kernel and divides its receptive field into regions according to direction and logarithmic distance. Adding distance levels expands the covered region exponentially. This organization encodes relative spatial structure while allowing a much larger single-layer receptive field without the corresponding parameter growth of an enlarged regular kernel.

The authors show how to implement the layer using log-polar space pooling followed by conventional convolution. They present it as a replacement for conventional convolution within network architectures, making the proposal a reusable layer rather than a complete task-specific model. Experiments across different tasks and datasets support its effectiveness. The central finding is that changing how spatial positions share representation can expand coverage while maintaining the number of parameters.
neurips-2022-log-polar-space-convolution.tldr: Log-polar convolutions organize spatial regions by direction and logarithmic distance to enlarge receptive fields without increasing parameter counts.

paragraphs: This paper introduces height as an architectural dimension alongside width and depth. Height describes recursive nesting: a hidden neuron is activated by another network of lower height. The resulting nested network, or NestNet, reduces to a conventional network when its height is one.

The authors prove constructive approximation results showing how nesting increases expressiveness. For 1-Lipschitz functions on the d-dimensional unit cube, a height-s ReLU NestNet with a parameter count proportional to n achieves error of order n raised to minus (s+1)/d. The stated optimal rate for standard ReLU networks with a comparable parameter count is n raised to minus 2/d.

The analysis also covers general continuous functions, with error characterized through their modulus of continuity. Numerical experiments illustrate advantages from the increased approximation power. The main contribution is a representational result: recursive activation networks can approximate the studied function classes more efficiently in parameter count. The constructive theorem concerns approximation capability, while the experiments provide empirical support for the architecture’s advantages.
neurips-2022-neural-network-architecture.tldr: NestNets introduce recursively nested activations, yielding stronger approximation rates than standard ReLU networks at comparable parameter counts.

paragraphs: Operator learning predicts functions from other functions, with applications to physical systems such as fluid flow. A common representation builds each predicted function as a linear combination of learned basis elements. However, a family of functions can have low intrinsic dimension while still requiring many elements for an accurate linear representation.

NOMAD addresses this mismatch with a nonlinear decoder. Its goal is to learn a compact, finite-dimensional representation of a nonlinear manifold within a function space. Allowing the decoder to be nonlinear gives the representation a way to follow the structure of the function family instead of expressing everything through a large linear basis.

The authors show accurate low-dimensional representations of solution manifolds for partial differential equations, with better performance than larger linear models. On a complex fluid-dynamics benchmark, NOMAD performs competitively with state-of-the-art operator-learning methods while using a significantly smaller model and lower training cost. These results support matching the decoder’s geometry to the structure of the target functions.
neurips-2022-nomad-nonlinear-manifold-de.tldr: NOMAD uses nonlinear decoders to represent physical solution families compactly, achieving competitive operator learning with smaller models.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models of evolutionary sequences are used to estimate molecular fitness and function. These applications rely on a relationship between how likely a sequence is under a model and how fit it is biologically. This paper investigates whether increasingly accurate sequence-probability estimates necessarily improve fitness estimates.

The authors prove that fitness cannot be uniquely identified from observational sequence data alone. In particular, the observations do not suffice to disentangle the fitness landscape from evolutionary history. This creates a fundamental information limit that cannot be removed simply by fitting the observed sequence distribution more accurately.

On real datasets, the analysis indicates with high confidence that even perfect density estimation in the infinite-data limit would produce poor fitness estimation. The authors attribute current models’ accurate fitness estimates to their misspecification: their imperfect representation of the sequence distribution is beneficial for this target. The finding challenges inevitable improvement through model and dataset scaling, while suggesting that fitness estimation needs objectives or strategies beyond density accuracy alone.
neurips-2022-non-identifiability-and-the.tldr: Fitness is not identifiable from sequence observations alone, and imperfect density models can estimate it better than perfect density estimation.

paragraphs: OmniVL brings image-language and video-language learning into one architecture. A shared transformer-based visual encoder handles both images and videos, enabling joint pretraining across the two input types. The paper reports benefits for both image and video tasks, extending beyond using image-language learning only to help video-language performance.

Its pretraining method separates spatial and temporal aspects of vision-language modeling. A unified contrastive loss also combines image-text, video-text, image-label, and video-label data. This allows the same training framework to use both supervised labels and noisier paired language data rather than relying on only one kind of supervision.

The resulting model supports visual classification, image or video retrieval from text, question answering, and captioning without additional task-specific adaptors. Across a broad range of downstream evaluations, it achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results at similar model sizes and data scales. The contribution is evidence that a shared architecture and coordinated training objective can support this variety while allowing image and video learning to benefit each other.
neurips-2022-omnivl-one-foundation-model.tldr: OmniVL jointly learns from images, videos, text, and labels in one architecture that supports diverse visual and language tasks.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching requires choosing matches as graph information arrives. This paper studies algorithms that additionally receive predictions of node degrees, potentially derived from prior data or modeling assumptions. Its proposed greedy rule, MinPredictedDegree, uses predicted degrees of the offline nodes to guide matching decisions.

The strongest result applies to a specific stochastic graph model: the bipartite Chung–Lu–Vu model with known expected offline degrees used as predictions. Within this setting, MinPredictedDegree stochastically dominates every other online algorithm. For the symmetric case where online nodes are identical, the authors derive a competitive ratio of at least 0.7299.

For graphs with power-law degree distributions, the method frequently finds matchings nearly as large as a true maximum matching. An extensive empirical evaluation also finds favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art online matching algorithms. These results show that degree information can be highly useful, while keeping the optimality claim tied to the specified graph model and the use of its expected degrees as predictions.
neurips-2022-optimal-online-bipartite-ma.tldr: MinPredictedDegree uses degree predictions for online matching and is optimal under a specified stochastic graph model with known expected degrees.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, value factorization connects the value of a team’s joint action to components that support individual decisions. Existing approaches can restrict which joint value functions they represent, alongside difficulties with sample efficiency and approximation error. ResQ introduces residual functions to address these problems.

The method masks selected state-action value pairs and rewrites the joint value function as a main function plus a residual function. The authors show that this construction can find an optimal joint policy for any state-action value function. It applies both to methods using expected values and to methods representing stochastic values.

The theoretical results establish the individual-global-max principle and its distributional counterpart without representation limitations. These principles connect individual maximizing choices to joint maximizing behavior, making the factorization useful for coordinated decisions. Experiments on matrix games, predator-prey, and StarCraft report better results than multiple expected-value and stochastic-value factorization methods. Thus, the paper combines a broad representational result with empirical evidence of improved performance in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2022-resq-a-residual-q-function-.tldr: ResQ uses residual value functions to support optimal joint policies without the representation restrictions of existing value factorizations.

paragraphs: Domain-incremental learning asks a model to learn across successive domains while retaining performance on earlier ones. S-Prompting tackles the resulting forgetting by learning separate prompts for each domain with pretrained transformers. It does not require storing exemplars from previous domains, which are commonly used by continual-learning methods.

Training uses a single cross-entropy loss, and inference uses a simple nearest-neighbor operation to identify the relevant domain. The paper develops both an image-prompt approach and a language-image prompt approach. Independent prompt learning gives each domain its own adaptation while keeping the overall procedure simple.

The reported parameter increase is 0.03% per domain. Across three standard domain-incremental tasks, the strongest approach achieves an average relative improvement of about 30% over the best compared exemplar-free methods. It also exceeds the best compared methods using exemplars by about 6% on average. These are relative empirical improvements on the studied tasks, supporting separate domain prompts as a scalable way to substantially reduce forgetting.
neurips-2022-s-prompts-learning-with-pre.tldr: S-Prompting learns independent domain prompts for pretrained transformers, substantially reducing forgetting without storing past examples.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent systems often train centrally and then let agents act separately. Such methods can struggle to generalize immediately when team membership changes or agents have different amounts of observable information. Self-Organized Group addresses these issues by organizing agents into temporary communication groups.

The mechanism has two parts: conductor election and message summary. At regular intervals of T time steps, a selected set of conductors forms temporary groups. Followers communicate only with their own conductor. Each conductor summarizes the incoming messages and distributes the summary to its group, supporting coordinated scheduling among the members.

This structure makes group formation and information exchange part of the coordination mechanism, rather than assuming a permanently fixed team arrangement. The paper reports zero-shot generalization to changing numbers of agents and varying partial observability. Experiments on mainstream multi-agent benchmarks show superior performance for the proposed approach. The findings support periodically reorganized, summarized communication as a practical way to handle the kinds of team and observation changes studied.
neurips-2022-self-organized-group-for-co.tldr: Self-Organized Group uses elected conductors and summarized messages to coordinate agents and generalize to changing teams and observability.

paragraphs: Detecting salient objects in sparsely annotated videos requires learning from frames without labels. Pseudo labels provide predicted annotations for those frames, but their mistakes can mislead training. This paper studies both how incorrect predictions can help improve pseudo-label generation and how remaining noise can be screened out.

The proposed Uncertainty-Guided Pseudo Label Generator uses information between frames to promote temporal consistency. It also strengthens learning on difficult scenarios to make the generated labels more robust. These mechanisms address complementary problems: maintaining coherent predictions through a video and improving predictions where the model is more likely to struggle.

The authors then introduce adversarial learning to handle noise that remains in the improved pseudo labels and support their positive contribution during training. Evaluations cover DAVIS, FBMS, MCL, ViSal, and SegTrack-V2. The method outperforms the existing semi-supervised comparison and some fully supervised methods across those benchmarks. The findings support improving and filtering predicted supervision as a way to learn effectively from limited video annotations.
neurips-2022-semi-supervised-video-salie.tldr: Uncertainty-guided, temporally consistent pseudo labels and adversarial noise handling improve salient-object detection with sparse video annotations.

paragraphs: Monotone data follow an ordering constraint: increasing inputs should not decrease outputs. This paper studies how efficiently neural networks can exactly fit such datasets while preserving monotonicity through nonnegative parameters and threshold units. The central questions concern how much depth and how many neurons this requires.

The authors show that some monotone datasets cannot be interpolated by a depth-two network of this kind. In contrast, every monotone dataset with n points in d dimensions has an interpolating depth-four network of size O(nd). This yields a depth-four construction that can approximate every monotone function on the unit cube arbitrarily well, improving the previous depth requirement of d plus one.

The paper also identifies a potential cost of enforcing positivity. Using results from Boolean circuit complexity, it shows that this inductive bias can cause a super-polynomial increase in neuron count when approximating monotone functions. Together, the results establish broad sufficiency of shallow fixed-depth constructions while showing that monotonic parameter constraints can still carry a substantial size penalty.
neurips-2022-size-and-depth-of-monotone-.tldr: Depth-four monotone networks can fit any finite monotone dataset, but positive-parameter constraints can impose substantial neuron-count costs.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning has produced many algorithms, but measuring progress requires trustworthy comparisons between them. This paper examines how the field evaluates those algorithms through a detailed meta-analysis of 75 papers accepted from 2016 to 2022. It reports concerning trends that make the apparent rate of progress harder to judge.

The authors combine findings from this analysis with applicable recommendations from research on single-agent reinforcement learning. From these sources, they propose a standardized performance-evaluation protocol for cooperative MARL. The contribution therefore concerns how evidence for algorithmic progress is produced and compared, rather than introducing another learning algorithm.

They argue that broad adoption would improve research validity and credibility, make replication and reproducibility easier, and enable sounder comparisons across papers over time. These benefits are presented as consequences of adoption, not as outcomes already established across the field. The authors also release the meta-analysis data and open-source evaluation tools, giving future researchers resources for examining evaluation practices and applying the proposed approach.
neurips-2022-towards-a-standardised-perf.tldr: A meta-analysis of 75 cooperative MARL papers motivates a standardized protocol for more credible and reproducible performance comparisons.

paragraphs: Equilibria are useful components in multi-agent algorithms, but computing them for a normal-form game can take an unpredictable amount of time or fail to converge. This paper proposes a Neural Equilibrium Solver that approximately solves games through a specially designed equivariant neural network.

The network is designed to cover games of a fixed shape, providing speed and deterministic computation. The paper also introduces a flexible framework for selecting among equilibria, with criteria such as minimizing relative entropy or maximizing welfare. This addresses both finding an equilibrium and determining which equilibrium the solver should prefer.

Training does not require generating supervised examples of solved games. The authors also report strong zero-shot generalization to larger games, extending empirical usefulness beyond the fixed-shape formulation. The outputs remain approximate solutions, and the larger-game result is a demonstrated generalization finding. The paper argues that combining fast inference, explicit selection preferences, and training without supervised solutions makes the solver a useful component for a range of multi-agent algorithms.
neurips-2022-turbocharging-solution-conc.tldr: A neural equilibrium solver produces fast approximate game solutions without supervised training examples and shows zero-shot generalization to larger games.
